title: The Hand Krishna Held Back
story:
The hospitality had been refused, the challenge all but spoken, and now the king of Magadha asked his own question before anyone else could. He did not recollect, Jarasandha said, ever acting injuriously toward his guests; even searching his memory with care, he could not find the injury he was supposed to have done them. "When I have never done ye an injury, why do ye regard me, who am innocent, as your foe? Answer me truly, for this is the rule followed by the honest."

Krishna's answer changed the air of the hall. It was not of his own will that he had come, he said; a certain person, at the head of a royal line, had sent him and his companions against the king. "Thou hast brought many of the Kshatriyas of the world as captives to thy city. Having perpetrated that wicked wrong, how dost thou regard thyself as innocent?" He spoke of kings treated with cruelty, gathered together and kept for a sacrifice to the god Rudra. "The slaughter of human beings as sacrifice unto the gods is never seen. Why dost thou seek to perform a sacrifice unto god Sankara by slaughtering human beings? Thou art addressing persons belonging to thy own order as animals fit for sacrifice."

Then he told them plainly who stood before him. "Know that we are certainly not Brahmanas. I am Hrishikesha, otherwise called Sauri, and these two heroes among men are the sons of Pandu. O king of Magadha, we challenge thee. Fight standing before us. Either set free all the monarchs, or go thou to the abode of Yama." He spoke of what waited for warriors who died in open fight — heaven, the sure consequence, the triumph of Indra himself won by vanquishing the Asuras — and of kings like Damvodhava, Kartavirya, Uttara and Vrihadratha, who had met destruction along with all their forces for disregarding their superiors. "Don't disregard others, O king. Valour dwelleth in every man. There are many men whose valour may be equal or superior to thine. Cast off thy superiority and pride in the presence of those that are thy equals."

Jarasandha's answer was unshaken. He never made a captive of a king without first vanquishing him, he said; every one of the monarchs kept in his city had been defeated in open war. It was the duty of his order, as he understood it, to bring others under sway by the exhibition of prowess and then to treat them as slaves. "Having gathered these monarchs with the intention of offering them as sacrifices unto the god, how shall I, from fear, liberate them today?" He would not bargain, and he would not bend: troops against troops, he said, or alone against one, or against two, or against three.

Now came the moment when the brothers might have fallen on him together. Krishna alone was more than a match for the king of Magadha; the strength of the descendants of Madhu could have ended the matter there and then. But the lord Sauri, ever devoted to truth, kept in view the command of Brahma, and remembered that the ruler of Magadha was destined to be slain in battle by Bhima, and not by a descendant of Madhu. He desired not to slay the king himself. He drew back his own hand, and left the king to Bhima.

The son of Pandu stepped forward to meet the king of Magadha, and the long duel began — a fight in which Krishna would take no part, because destiny had written this death with a particular name on it, and he would not write over it with his own.
reflection: The hinge of the episode is Krishna's restraint — the king of Magadha stands within his reach, yet he will not take what destiny has assigned to another hand. His power shows itself as much in what he refuses to do as in what he does.
next_story_tease: But even as the duel began, a new enemy was already marching against Mathura — the Yavana king Kalayavana.
hero_scene: Bhima stepping forward to face Jarasandha in the middle of the great hall, while Krishna stands back with arms folded, deliberately refusing a fight that destiny has assigned to another.
visual_elements: Bhima and Jarasandha facing each other
Krishna standing aside, withholding his hand
